An original visual language

Four non-ASCII directions for a 3D-authored horror world, with mockups, references and production trade-offs.

My recommendation: porcelain night

For your 3D-first workflow, I would test a fired, chipped, repaired miniature world. It gives simple models a strong material identity and lets reflections do real visual work. Woodcut weather is the runner-up if you want a much more graphic, nearly monochrome image.

These are AI-generated look-development studies, not engine renders or production assets. The existing 3D screenshot was supplied as a layout reference; the generator changed some geometry and framing. The studies do not prove animation, lighting fidelity, renderer compatibility, or performance. No game code was changed.

Porcelain night

A fired, chipped, repaired world. Best fit for 3D-first production.

Visual language
Glazed ivory and celadon shells, terracotta chips, blunt bevels, dark matte ground. A clay-like player rather than a realistic person. Shape and specular response do the work, not typography.
Our own rule
Only the damaged edges reveal warm clay beneath the cold glaze. Repair staples and deliberately oversized tile seams form a repeatable construction language.
Rain, wind and reflections
Rain darkens the matte surfaces and gathers into black glassy water. Wind bends sparse wire-like forms. Reflections stay smooth while chips catch small sharp highlights. Optional held animation poses can suggest miniatures; input and camera should remain responsive.
Blender work
Beveled modular meshes, imperfect silhouettes, a small kit of chipped edges. Bake procedural crack/roughness/normal masks rather than generating individual 2D illustrations.
Godot work
Material-specific roughness and normal maps, localized lamps, the existing planar reflection technique. No real-time ray tracing is required. Mobile cost still needs measurement.
Main risk
Can become cute toy art, or drift into generic realistic ruined tiles. Keep the forms thick and sculptural, the prop count low, and damage sparse. The concept image is more polished than a first real-time prototype will be.
Reference, attribution, and what not to copy

Harold Halibut shows the tactile value of handmade miniature construction. Borrow material coherence, not its characters, retro-future setting, or production-heavy physical fabrication.

Harold Halibut screenshot — Slow Bros.; from the official website. Read the primary source.

Woodcut weather

Black ink, ivory incisions, and almost no color. Strongest graphic alternative.

Visual language
Large black masses cut by broad irregular ivory marks. Stone joints are carved lines; trees are expressive silhouettes; water breaks the reflected forms into horizontal cuts. A tiny amber accent is reserved for lamps.
Our own rule
Each material has a different cut direction and pressure: masonry is block-like, cloth is broad and soft, water is horizontal. Never use an evenly spaced character or dot grid.
Rain, wind and reflections
Rain becomes sparse white incisions. Wind moves the silhouettes, not a screen noise texture. A moving light opens or closes carved white regions. Water distorts the actual reflected shape before its ink treatment.
Blender work
Simple geometry plus a small reusable library of engraved masks and UVs. Art effort is in choosing purposeful cuts, not drawing every full scene.
Godot work
A restrained lighting ramp, stable object/UV-space carving masks, selective silhouettes, and an ink treatment for the reflection pass. A screen-only brightness filter would miss the identity and can shimmer.
Main risk
Small shapes can merge or flicker under camera motion. It also lives in a familiar monochrome indie-horror family. Preserve a clear player silhouette and a minimum size for meaningful details.
Reference, attribution, and what not to copy

Mundaun demonstrates authored surface marks on a 3D world; its developer describes hand-penciled environments. Our proposal is coarse relief-print cuts, not its pencil textures or Alpine folklore. Woodcut reference: Frans Masereel’s Skyscrapers, MSK Gent.

Mundaun screenshot — Hidden Fields; from Annapurna Interactive’s game page. Read the primary source.

MSK Gent: Frans Masereel, Skyscrapers (1926), woodcut on paper. A reference for broad relief-print contrast, not an asset to reproduce.

Cut-paper nocturne

A layered stage set, not low-poly stone with a paper texture.

Visual language
Overlapping card slabs, exposed corrugated edges, slotted flat trees, folded strips for reeds, dusty burgundy against charcoal blue. A foil-like pool contains broad cut-shaped reflected bands.
Our own rule
Thickness and joinery are always visible. Shadows reveal the layers; folds tell you how the object was constructed. Matte slabs remain large and quiet.
Rain, wind and reflections
Wind bends hinges and curled strips. Rain is a sparse set of angled slivers. Reflections can be simplified into a few broad moving bands. Avoid full paper/cloth simulation in the first demo.
Blender work
Extruded planes, folded meshes, a few cardstock edge textures, and reusable connectors. Camera-facing cheats need limits; exposed reverse sides must still look intentionally constructed.
Godot work
Simple materials and vertex bends, controlled shadows, and the existing water camera with restrained quantization. A constrained three-quarter camera is easier than unrestricted orbit.
Main risk
May look like cheerful craft or ordinary low-poly art. The stronger second study makes the corrugated edges and large wall sheets explicit. A moving-camera test must prove thickness survives.
Reference, attribution, and what not to copy

Tearaway’s creative lead discusses fold, flex, peel and tactile construction. Borrow the discipline of building from a material, not its bright folklore world, protagonist, or fourth-wall interaction.

Physical Tearaway papercraft reference photo — Media Molecule / PlayStation Blog. Not a gameplay screenshot. Read the primary source.

Afterimage

The world remembers light. Most experimental; highest rendering risk.

Visual language
Incomplete cyan-white contour deposits over almost untouched darkness. Large faces remain absent. The player is a small solid anchor; a pool briefly holds a clearer ghost of nearby architecture.
Our own rule
The important proposed rule is light memory: illumination leaves a slowly fading exposure on surfaces. This cannot be demonstrated by a still image; without it the study is only a point-cloud-like look.
Rain, wind and reflections
Rain leaves short fading strokes; exposed surfaces persist after a lamp moves away. Water could retain a brief luminous residue. Keep movement and navigable edges readable; do not add a scanner just to justify the visual effect.
Blender work
Surface meshes, simplified edge carriers, and UV/layout data for a possible persistent exposure field. Sparse marks must be tied to the world, not randomly replaced every frame.
Godot work
First test stable sparse surface marks and edge reveal. Genuine light memory needs a persistent exposure/history representation and separate handling for moving objects. This is a new R&D task, not a one-shader promise.
Main risk
Resembles Scanner Sombre unless the memory behavior is strong. Navigation can become unreadable; history and transparent overdraw may be expensive. Highest risk for small/offline mobile scope.
Reference, attribution, and what not to copy

Scanner Sombre establishes the legibility and atmosphere of incomplete scanned geometry. Our proposal must avoid its rainbow LIDAR/scanner identity and prove a different temporal rule.

Scanner Sombre screenshot — Introversion Software; official Steam store media. Read the primary source.

A style is not enough; change the subject matter too

Changing the shader while keeping a ruined arch, reflective pond, skeletal trees and amber lamps would still leave a recognizable compositional debt. The courtyard above is only a comparison rig. I would move the actual world toward a damaged municipal bathhouse or pumping station: oversized glazed panels, exposed clay edges, repeated pipe forms, sparse repair staples, and black reflective water. No medieval fantasy iconography or borrowed characters.

New-setting concept, also AI-generated. This is an art-direction proposal, not a plot. Its exact lighting and material finish must be re-established in a real-time scene.

The visual contract

  • Three dominant surface families: glazed shell, exposed fired-clay core, and quiet matte structure.
  • Deliberate thick bevels and oversized joins. No realistic microdetail everywhere.
  • Wear exposes the underlying material; it is not decorative random grime.
  • One reserved warm light family against cold surfaces, with generous unlit space.
  • Water is a calm black plane until weather, a footstep or a reflection disturbs it.
  • No glyph grid, rainbow LIDAR, fantasy ruin motifs, or compulsory glitch effects.

Production trade-offs

Relative judgments for this small Blender/Godot project, not measured budgets or benchmarks.

What you would actually be choosing
DirectionMain production workRendering riskBest reason to choose it
Porcelain nightModerate model/material work; little bespoke 2D artModerate: wetness, highlights and reflection costTactile 3D identity; strongest fit for simple procedural models
Woodcut weatherModerate mark authoring and shader tuningModerate: stability, merged silhouettesBold graphic horror; far from a character-grid image
Cut-paper nocturneLow-to-moderate modular geometry; explicit thicknessLower for a constrained camera; simulation must stay limitedManageable small/offline-game art scope
AfterimageHigh renderer R&D; sparse world assetsHighest: exposure history, depth, navigationA distinctive temporal behavior, if proven in motion

What I would avoid

Generic PS1/VHS corruption as the whole identity; painterly post-processing that demands lots of bespoke illustrations; or “the same ASCII scene with a new font.” Each can be useful locally, but none solves your request for a coherent world of our own.

A decision, not another implementation yet

My proposed next test is Porcelain night in a tiny bathhouse scene: one tile module, one wall, one lamp, one pool, one moving player, rain and a single wind-reactive object. An 8–10 second camera/movement loop should prove that the material remains readable, the reflection is convincing and the shapes do not turn into generic realistic tiles. If you prefer graphic rather than tactile, test Woodcut weather instead.

No direction is approved yet. Existing demo and PR were left unchanged. A new art pass should wait for your choice. None of these broad media is invented here; the originality would come from consistent construction, material behavior, composition and subject matter rather than a claim of a first-ever style.
